paper_metadata.title: Oxidation Behaviour of New Nickel-Base Superalloys with Varying Aluminium: Niobium Ratio

evidence.quote: New Ni-base superalloys with higher temperature capability are required for future, more efficient gas turbine engines.

The microstructures of the polycrystalline Ni-base superalloys used for turbine discs comprise a solid solution matrix phase γ (Ni—cubic, A1), strengthened with a dispersion of ordered precipitates, most commonly γ′ (Ni3Al—cubic, L12), but in some Nb-bearing alloys also the metastable γ″ (Ni3Nb—tetragonal, D022)

The microstructures of the polycrystalline Ni-base superalloys used for turbine discs comprise a solid solution matrix phase γ (Ni—cubic, A1), strengthened with a dispersion of ordered precipitates, most commonly γ′ (Ni3Al—cubic, L12), but in some Nb-bearing alloys also the metastable γ″ (Ni3Nb—tetragonal, D022)

It should also be noted that some fine elongated precipitates (on the same scale as the γ′) are visible in the bulk of Alloy 1, likely to be γ″, which is known to form in alloys with elevated Nb content such as IN718 [3, 82] as well as the dual-superlattice alloys that this alloy series is based on [76, 83, 84].

As confirmed by the localised Nb enrichment in the elemental concentration maps, there is extensive precipitation of the δ phase after long-term oxidation exposure, which is confined to the γ′ denuded zone at 700 °C, and extends into the bulk at 800 °C (in Alloys 1–3).
The elemental concentration maps indicate the presence of a continuous chromium enriched layer, corresponding with enrichment in the oxygen map.

There is clear evidence of Al enrichment in the overscale, coincident with the Cr enrichment. However, additional Al enrichment is seen beneath the overscale associated with the intrusions observed in the SE images.

attributes.composition: rich in Cr, Nb and Mo

evidence.quote: There is also evidence of globular precipitates with elevated Cr content that extend deep into the bulk material that were not apparent in the SE images. These globular precipitates are also rich in Nb and Mo (see supplementary information). The composition and morphology of these precipitates is consistent with them being carbides, which are known to form in Ni-base superalloys.
Also visible from the elemental concentration maps is a sub-surface region depleted in Cr, with the depth of this region decreasing from approximately. 1.5 μm in Alloy 1, to 0.5 μm in Alloy 4.

The average grain sizes determined by the linear intercept method on data acquired via EBSD were 20 ± 12, 29 ± 18, 23 ± 14 and 60 ± 50 μm for Alloys 1–4 , respectively, (for further details please see supplementary information).
